title: Grade 4 Science — Tue, Jun 24
description: Food and Digestion — Day 2 of 5: Oesophagus, stomach and gastric digestion
subject: science

questions.question: After food is swallowed, it travels down a muscular tube to the stomach. This tube is called the:
questions.explanation: The oesophagus (food pipe) is a muscular tube connecting the throat to the stomach. It pushes food down using wave-like muscle contractions called peristalsis.

questions.question: The stomach stores food and mixes it with digestive juices. Roughly how long does food stay in the stomach?
questions.explanation: Food stays in the stomach for about 2–4 hours while it is mixed and broken down. The stomach churns food and mixes it with gastric juice.

questions.question: Gastric juice is produced by the stomach. What does it contain?
options: Hydrochloric acid and the enzyme pepsin
questions.explanation: Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid (HCl) which kills germs and creates an acidic environment, and pepsin — an enzyme that begins protein digestion.

questions.question: The semi-liquid mixture of food and gastric juices in the stomach is called:
questions.explanation: Once food is churned with gastric juice in the stomach, it becomes a semi-liquid called chyme. This is passed into the small intestine.

questions.question: Peristalsis is the movement that pushes food through the digestive system. It is caused by:
options: Wave-like muscular contractions of the digestive tube walls
questions.explanation: Peristalsis = wave-like contractions of smooth muscles in the oesophagus, stomach and intestines. It pushes food along the digestive tract regardless of gravity (you can eat upside down!).

questions.question: The stomach has a thick lining to protect itself from acid. What would happen if the lining were damaged?
options: The stomach acid would digest the stomach wall, causing a stomach ulcer
The stomach would produce more acid
questions.explanation: If the protective mucus lining breaks down, stomach acid attacks the stomach wall, causing painful ulcers. The stomach must protect itself from its own acid.

questions.question: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach serves which TWO purposes?
options: Kills harmful bacteria in food and creates an acidic environment for pepsin to work
questions.explanation: HCl in stomach: (1) kills germs/bacteria that entered with food (protection), (2) creates the low pH environment that pepsin needs to digest protein. Dual role: defence + digestion.

questions.question: How does the stomach churn food?
options: It uses teeth at its entrance
Muscular walls of the stomach contract and relax repeatedly, mixing food with gastric juice
It blows air into the food
The liver churns food for the stomach
questions.explanation: The stomach has three layers of muscle that contract in different directions. This vigorous churning mixes food with gastric juice thoroughly, producing chyme.

questions.question: Why does the oesophagus NOT begin digesting food as it passes through?
options: The oesophagus does not produce digestive enzymes — its job is only transport (pushing food to the stomach)
It contains a lot of acid
questions.explanation: The oesophagus is a transport tube only. It has no digestive enzymes and produces no acid. Digestion begins in the mouth (starch) and continues in the stomach (protein).

questions.question: A child drinks a glass of milk. Where does protein digestion of the milk begin?
questions.explanation: Milk contains protein. Protein digestion begins in the stomach using pepsin (activated by HCl). The mouth only digests starch (via amylase). The oesophagus does no digestion.

questions.question: Antacids (like ENO or Digene) are used when someone has acidity/heartburn. How do they work?
options: They add more acid to the stomach
They are bases/alkalis that neutralise excess stomach acid, relieving discomfort
They stop the stomach from churning
They remove food from the stomach
questions.explanation: Antacids are mild alkalis (e.g., magnesium hydroxide, calcium carbonate). They neutralise excess HCl in the stomach: acid + alkali → salt + water. This relieves acidity and heartburn.

questions.question: Vomiting (reverse peristalsis) is the body's way of expelling harmful substances. What does this tell us about the digestive system?
options: The digestive system has defensive mechanisms — it can reverse direction to protect the body from poisons
Vomiting is only caused by overeating
The oesophagus cannot be used in reverse
questions.explanation: Vomiting is reverse peristalsis — the stomach forces contents back up through the oesophagus and out. This is a protective mechanism to expel toxins, poisons or spoiled food before they are absorbed.

questions.question: The pyloric sphincter is a ring of muscle at the stomach exit. What does it do?
options: It controls the rate at which chyme passes from the stomach into the small intestine
questions.explanation: The pyloric sphincter opens and closes to regulate how much chyme enters the small intestine at a time. This controlled release ensures the small intestine is not overwhelmed.

questions.question: Compare: Why does the stomach need thick muscular walls while the oesophagus needs thinner walls?
options: Stomach needs thick walls for churning and protection from acid; oesophagus only needs to propel food by peristalsis — less force needed
Oesophagus needs thicker walls since it carries food further
questions.explanation: Stomach: 3-layer muscles for vigorous churning + thick mucus lining for acid protection. Oesophagus: simpler 2-layer muscles sufficient for peristaltic transport. Structure matches function.

questions.question: Sequence the digestive journey of a roti from the moment it enters the mouth: Mouth → ___ → ___ → ___
questions.explanation: Correct sequence: Mouth (chewing, amylase) → Oesophagus (transport) → Stomach (churning, pepsin, HCl) → Small intestine (absorption). This is the standard digestive pathway.
